common_name: Bishop of Oxford Dahlia (Salmon-Peach Peony-Flowered Bronze-Leaf Dahlia)

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep after soil has warmed; like its Bishop series siblings, foliage emerges near-black before settling to deep bronze-purple.

directions: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep once the soil has warmed in spring. A member of the Bishop series alongside 'Bishop of Llandaff' and 'Bishop of York', this cultivar carries the same deeply cut, near-black bronze-purple foliage but opens semi-double, peony-form blooms in soft salmon-peach with a warm apricot glow toward the center. Flowers measure roughly 3-4 inches across and are held on sturdy burgundy stems from midsummer into fall, with the open form drawing bees and other pollinators more readily than fully double cultivars. Its modest height suits mixed borders and large containers without heavy staking.

common_name: Bishop of Canterbury Dahlia (Vermilion-Red Peony-Flowered Bronze-Leaf Dahlia)

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep after soil has warmed; the dark bronze foliage of this Bishop series member sets off its vivid red-orange blooms.

directions: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep in well-drained soil once frost danger has passed. Bishop of Canterbury carries the finely divided, near-black bronze foliage typical of the Bishop series, but its semi-double, peony-form flowers open in a hot vermilion-red rather than the gold or peach of its siblings, giving the plant strong garden contrast. Blooms open from midsummer through early fall and hold well on sturdy stems, making the plant useful both as a garden accent and a cut flower. Feed lightly through the season and deadhead spent blooms to keep new flowers coming.

common_name: Bishop of Dover Dahlia (White Peony-Flowered Bronze-Leaf Dahlia)

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep after soil has warmed; the near-white blooms of this Bishop series member stand out sharply against its dark foliage.

directions: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep once the soil has warmed in spring. The palest member of the Bishop series, Bishop of Dover pairs the group's signature deeply cut, near-black bronze-purple foliage with semi-double, peony-form flowers that open creamy white and soften further as they age, giving the plant a striking light-on-dark presence in the border. It blooms from midsummer to frost on sturdy burgundy stems and works especially well as a pale accent among the darker-flowered Bishop cultivars. Deadhead regularly and lift tubers before hard frost in cold-winter regions.

common_name: Happy Single Wink Dahlia (Pink-and-White Bicolor Single Bloom over Bronze Foliage)

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep after last frost; Happy Single Wink, part of the Happy Single series, opens pink-purple blooms fading to a white center over dark bronze foliage.

directions: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep with the growth eye facing up after the last frost. Happy Single Wink belongs to the compact, garden-friendly Happy Single series and bears single, open blooms in vivid pink-purple that lighten toward a near-white halo around the central disc, all held above dark bronze, finely cut foliage. The open flower form is highly attractive to bees and butterflies, and the well-branched, floriferous plants stay tidy enough for containers and small border edges. Deadhead spent flowers to prolong bloom and lift tubers after frost blackens the foliage in zones colder than 8.

common_name: Happy Single Date Dahlia (Wine-Red Single Bloom over Dark Bronze Foliage)

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep after last frost; Happy Single Date carries deep wine-red single blooms over near-black bronze foliage.

directions: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep with the growth eye up once the danger of frost has passed. This Happy Single series member produces rich wine-red, single blooms with a small gold-ringed disc, set against dark bronze-purple, finely divided foliage on a compact, well-branched plant. Its open bloom form is far more accessible to pollinators than double-flowered dahlias, and the shorter stature suits patio containers as readily as a mixed border. Deadhead through the season to keep flowers coming, and dig tubers for storage after the foliage is blackened by frost in zones below 8.

common_name: Happy Single Kiss Dahlia (Amber-Orange Bicolor Single Bloom over Bronze Foliage)

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep after last frost; Happy Single Kiss earned an RHS Award of Garden Merit for its reliable bedding performance.

directions: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep with the growth eye facing up after the last frost. Happy Single Kiss, an RHS Award of Garden Merit holder from the Happy Single series, produces amber-orange single blooms that deepen toward a warm red-orange center, held above dark, purple-bronze foliage on a compact, heavily branching plant. Its long bloom season and open flower form make it one of the more reliable bedding dahlias for attracting pollinators to a sunny border or large patio pot. Pinch young plants to encourage bushiness and deadhead regularly to sustain flowering into fall.

common_name: Hamari Gold Dahlia (Bronze-Orange Large Decorative Dahlia)

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep after soil has warmed; set a stake at planting time, as Hamari Gold's large blooms are heavy on tall stems.

directions: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep once the soil has warmed, staking at planting time to support the tall, sturdy stems. A long-standing favorite on the British show bench and an RHS Award of Garden Merit winner, Hamari Gold produces fully double, formal decorative blooms in warm bronze-orange that can reach 8 inches or more across with good culture. The vigorous, upright plant blooms from midsummer to frost and holds its color well in heat. Feed monthly and disbud side buds if larger show-quality blooms are wanted, then lift and store tubers after frost in all but the mildest climates.

common_name: Hamari Accord Dahlia (Soft Yellow Large Decorative Dahlia)

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep after soil has warmed; stake at planting time to support Hamari Accord's large, heavy blooms.

directions: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep once the soil has warmed, staking early to carry the weight of the large blooms. Bred as a companion to 'Hamari Gold', Hamari Accord is a fully double, formal decorative dahlia in soft primrose-yellow with broad, gently waved petals that can open to 8 inches across on a tall, vigorous plant. It flowers heavily from midsummer through fall and holds its form well in cool autumn weather, making it a dependable choice for both borders and the cutting garden. Feed regularly through the growing season and lift tubers for winter storage once frost blackens the foliage.

common_name: Wittemans Superba Dahlia (Butterscotch-Apricot Incurved Cactus Dahlia)

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep after soil has warmed; this heirloom Dutch cactus dahlia dates to the 1930s and still performs reliably in the garden today.

directions: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep once the soil has warmed, staking tall plants at planting time. Introduced in the Netherlands in the 1930s and still grown as a heritage cactus dahlia, Wittemans Superba produces narrow, curled, incurved petals in a warm butterscotch-apricot blend on a tall, willowy plant that blooms from midsummer to frost. Its slender petal form gives the flower a softer, more delicate look than modern broad-petaled cactus types, and the long stems make it a good choice for cutting. Deadhead spent blooms to extend flowering and dig tubers for storage before hard frost.

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep after soil has warmed; L'Ancresse is a Guernsey-raised waterlily dahlia named for a bay on the island.

directions: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep once the soil has warmed in spring. Raised on the island of Guernsey and named for one of its coastal bays, L'Ancresse carries the shallow, few-petaled waterlily form in soft blush pink shading to cream-white toward the center, giving the flower a luminous, watercolor quality. Long, strong stems and a moderate petal count make it a favorite among cut-flower growers, and the plant blooms freely from midsummer to frost with regular deadheading. Lift and store tubers after the foliage is blackened by frost in regions colder than zone 8.

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep after soil has warmed; Pam Howden is one of the most widely grown waterlily dahlias for cutting.

directions: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep once the soil has warmed in spring. Pam Howden is a British-bred waterlily dahlia whose shallow, gently cupped blooms shift from soft peach at the petal tips to a warm apricot-orange at the center, opening on strong, upright stems well suited to bouquets. It is among the most widely grown waterlily-type dahlias for cut-flower production thanks to its prolific, long-lasting blooms and good vase life. Deadhead regularly to keep flowers coming through the season and dig tubers for winter storage once frost blackens the foliage.

common_name: Jersey's Beauty Dahlia (Clear Pink Formal Decorative Dahlia)

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep after soil has warmed; Jersey's Beauty is a mid-20th-century American cultivar still ranked among the best cut-flower dahlias.

directions: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep once the soil has warmed, staking tall plants at planting time. Introduced in the 1950s, Jersey's Beauty remains one of the most celebrated formal decorative dahlias ever raised, prized for its clear, unfading rich pink blooms on long, strong, arrow-straight stems that hold up exceptionally well after cutting. The vigorous plant produces flowers in great abundance from midsummer through fall and remains a benchmark cut-flower variety against which newer pink decoratives are still measured. Feed monthly for best bloom size and lift tubers for storage before hard frost.

common_name: Miss Rose Fletcher Dahlia (Soft Shell-Pink Quilled Cactus Dahlia)

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep after soil has warmed; this 1930s heirloom cultivar is still grown for its softly quilled, incurved pink petals.

directions: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep once the soil has warmed in spring. A cultivar dating to the 1930s, Miss Rose Fletcher bears soft shell-pink blooms with narrow, gently incurved, quill-like petals that curl inward toward the center, giving each flower a delicate, ruffled softness distinct from stiffer modern cactus forms. It remains popular with heirloom collectors and cut-flower growers alike for its abundant, long-stemmed blooms produced from midsummer to frost. Deadhead spent flowers regularly and dig tubers for winter storage once frost blackens the foliage.

common_name: Vassio Meggos Dahlia (Giant Salmon-Bronze Exhibition Decorative Dahlia)

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep after soil has warmed; set a sturdy stake at planting time, as Vassio Meggos is a top exhibition giant needing strong support.

directions: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep once the soil has warmed, setting a sturdy stake or cage at planting time to support the massive flower heads. A perennial favorite on the exhibition show bench, Vassio Meggos produces giant, fully double decorative blooms in blended salmon, bronze, and soft apricot tones that can exceed 9-10 inches across under generous feeding and disbudding. The tall, vigorous plant needs rich soil, consistent moisture, and monthly fertilizing to reach show-quality size, and side buds should be removed early if the largest single blooms are the goal. Dig and store tubers after frost in all but the mildest climates.

common_name: Kenora Valentine Dahlia (Bright Red Small Decorative Dahlia)

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep after soil has warmed; Kenora Valentine is part of the widely grown Canadian Kenora series of exhibition dahlias.

directions: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep once the soil has warmed in spring. Part of the popular Kenora series of Canadian-bred dahlias, Kenora Valentine produces fully double, small decorative blooms in bright, unfading true red on an upright, well-branched plant that flowers heavily from midsummer to frost. Its compact bloom size and sturdy stems make it a favorite for both garden borders and the cutting bucket, and it holds its color well through hot weather. Deadhead regularly to sustain bloom and lift tubers for winter storage once frost blackens the foliage.

common_name: Bristol Stripe Dahlia (Red-and-White Flecked Ball Dahlia)

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep after soil has warmed; Bristol Stripe is a classic British show ball dahlia valued for its red-and-white flecked petals.

directions: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep once the soil has warmed in spring. A long-grown British show variety, Bristol Stripe produces densely packed, honeycombed ball-form blooms in rich red flecked and splashed with white, giving each flower a lively broken-color pattern rarely seen in solid-colored ball dahlias. The compact, sturdy plant blooms freely from midsummer to frost and holds its round form well both in the garden and in the vase. Deadhead spent blooms to keep new flowers coming and dig tubers for storage before hard frost in cold-winter regions.
